What happened on New Year's Eve
It's 2 January. Mara goes down to the bakery. Lena wants to hear everything about New Year's Eve: Mara was on the night shift in A&E, and Jonas wanted to propose to Clara right at midnight.
Happy New Year, Mara! How was New Year's Eve? Did you go to a party?
A party? No! I was on the night shift in A&E. It was the craziest night of my life.
From midnight on we had twenty patients in three hours. Burns, cuts, one man had a rocket in his sleeve…
Oh my God! And Jonas? Did he ask Clara? Grandpa told me. He can't keep a secret.
Ha! That's the best story. At one o'clock Jonas came into A&E. As a patient!
He was with Clara on the bank of the Spree. At midnight he took the ring out of his pocket and got down on one knee. At that very moment, a rocket exploded next to them.
Yes. He burned his hand, not badly, and the ring fell into the snow. They searched for half an hour, but they didn't find it.
Poor Jonas! And Clara? Did she say yes?
Wait, wait! I bandaged his hand. And then Clara took off her gloves. And what was in her glove? The ring!
Then she put it on her finger herself and said: “Yes. But next year we're celebrating New Year's Eve at home.” The whole of A&E clapped!
gone (“auf die Knie gehen” = to kneel down)
“hatte” (had) has “a”; “hätte” (would have, chap. 23) has “ä”. For now: hatte = “HAH-teh”.
“Silvester” = “zil-VES-ter”: the initial S = “z”, and the “v” here is read “v”.
The prefix “ver-” is short and unstressed: ver-LIE-ren, ver-GES-sen, ver-BRANNT.
For “to be” and “to have”, Germans almost always use the short form, the Präteritum, instead of the Perfekt when speaking:
How was your New Year's Eve? (more natural than “ist gewesen”)
The practical rule: SEIN, HABEN and the modal verbs → Präteritum (war, hatte, konnte). Almost all other verbs → Perfekt. That's how Germans speak.
As with the modals, ich and er have the same form and take no ending: ich war, er war.
Er hat den Ring rausgeholt. Sie hat die Handschuhe ausgezogen.
Er hat sich verbrannt. Ich habe es vergessen.
Die Rakete ist explodiert. Was ist passiert?
And the auxiliary: SEIN for movement and change of state (ist gefallen, ist gegangen, ist explodiert) and for “passieren”, “bleiben”; HABEN for everything else.
vor einer Woche / vor einem Jahr
a week ago / a year ago (vor + dative)
“vor” + time = “… ago”: “vor zwei Jahren” = two years ago. Don't confuse it with “seit” = “for, since” (still going on): “seit zwei Jahren” = for two years.

On the thirty-first of December, at nine p.m., Mara's shift in A&E began. Outside it was cold, minus five degrees, and there was snow. All over the city, people had bought rockets, bangers and champagne.

Dr Yılmaz was there too. She had brought coffee for the whole team, a huge thermos, and in the afternoon Lena had sent a basket of “Berliner”: jam doughnuts, which in Berlin are traditionally eaten on New Year's Eve.
Enjoy the quiet, colleagues. At midnight the madness begins.

She was right. Until half past eleven everything was quiet. A man had eaten too much potato salad, a woman had cut her finger while cooking. Then, at midnight, the whole city could be heard through the windows: thousands of rockets, music, shouting. The sky above Berlin was red, green and gold.

Mara had no time to look. At ten past twelve the first patient arrived: a young man with a burn on his arm. Then two girls who had slipped on the ice. Then a man who had lit a rocket in his hand instead of putting it in a bottle.
At one o'clock the door opened and Mara saw a familiar face. Jonas! He was holding his right hand up in the air. Next to him stood a young woman with red hair and a green woolly hat. She looked pale.
Jonas! What are you doing here? You're off today!
Don't ask. Mara, this is Clara. Clara, this is Mara, the best nurse in Berlin.
Mara looked at the hand. It was a slight burn, not dangerous, but it certainly hurt. While she cooled and bandaged his hand, Clara told the story.

We were at the Oberbaumbrücke. At midnight Jonas suddenly said: “Clara, I have to tell you something.” And then he got down on one knee, in the middle of the snow. I didn't understand a thing. I thought he had slipped!
I had the little ring box in my hand. And at that very moment some idiot next to us lit a battery of rockets. One flew off sideways, straight onto my hand. The box fell and the ring disappeared.
We searched in the snow, with the light from my phone. For half an hour! And Jonas kept saying “I'm sorry, I'm sorry”. His hand was red. Then I said: that's it, we're going to the hospital.
Mara finished the bandage. Dr Yılmaz came by, took a look at the hand and said: “Two weeks without night shifts, Mr Weber. And no rockets. Ever.”

Clara wanted to put her gloves back on. She had taken them off on the bridge, to search the snow better, and then she had quickly stuffed them into her jacket pocket. When she put on her left glove, she stopped. There was something in it. Something small, hard, round.
She took the glove off again and shook it. A small gold ring fell onto the A&E couch. It had fallen into the glove while she was searching in the snow.
For a moment there was complete silence. Jonas looked at the ring, then at Clara, then at the ring again. He wanted to kneel down, but Clara held him back.
No, not on your knees again! Who knows what else might happen. Yes, Jonas. Yes, I want to marry you. But next year we're celebrating New Year's Eve at home. On the sofa. Without rockets.

She put the ring on her finger herself. It fitted perfectly. And then something happened that Mara had never experienced in her whole career as a nurse: the whole of A&E clapped. The doctors, the nurses, the patients, even the man with the rocket.

At six in the morning the shift ended. Mara went home on the M1. The streets were full of rocket debris and empty bottles, but the sky was clear and pink. The light was already on in the bakery. Lena was standing in the doorway, with two coffees in her hands.
Lena, you won't believe what happened last night.
